..A busy weather pattern through the weekend for 
southeast Arizona. The upper air pattern currently features 
southwesterly flow as an active subtropical jet pattern takes hold. 
The first of two significant weather systems will impact southeast 
Arizona today. A pre-cursor disturbance has already resulted in 
scattered showers and thunderstorms last night, with showers and 
thunderstorms persisting early this morning as broader lift 
increases across the region under broad diffluent flow and 
increasing 850-700mb moisture convergence. In the last hour a round 
of thunderstorms moved through Tucson producing a quick localized 
0.5" to 1 inch of rain and some small hail. Latest SPC mesoanalysis 
shows MUCAPE around 1000 J/KG helping to support elevated 
convection. CAMs have really struggled this morning picking up on 
any of this activity, so have made short term modifications to the 
forecast to maintain scattered showers and thunderstorms through the 
morning hours before more widespread shower and thunderstorm 
activity moves in this afternoon. This activity will be aided by the 
combination of broad scale lift in the left front quadrant of the 
250mb jet and deep lower level moisture with strong 850-700mb 
moisture convergence. Still some uncertainty in terms of just how 
much solar insolation we'll see to increase surface based 
instability but should be enough warming to generate around 500-1000 
J/KG of SBCAPE which combined with modest 0-6km bulk shear around 30 
kts will be enough to result in the potential for a few stronger to 
marginally severe thunderstorms. SPC continues to outline our area 
in a marginal risk today for severe thunderstorms with strong wind 
gusts and hail the main threats. We're also in a marginal risk from 
WPC for excessive rain north of Tucson today. The most common 
additional rain amounts today through this evening will be 0.25" to 
0.75", though given the convective nature of the precipitation, some 
areas will see less and others more. Higher precipitation amounts 
can be expected in areas that see repeating rounds of thunderstorms 
which is most likely north to northeast of Tucson. In this case, 
isolated areas of 1 to 2 inches of rain (with isolated flash 
flooding as well) are expected with the probability of 1 inch or 
more of rain averaging about 20 percent for any single location. 

While the area remains under southwesterly flow aloft on Saturday, 
we'll generally be between systems with limited large scale lift. 
However, given the moisture still in place (0.75" to 1" PWAT), 
isolated shower activity is expected (10 to 20 percent chances 
during the day), with any precipitation short lived under individual 
showers. Thereafter, more widespread rain chances start to ramp up 
as the evening progresses Saturday night on the leading edge of the 
next more significant weather system. 

A more potent subtropical weather system the moves into and through 
our region Sunday through Sunday night. This will bring near record 
to record levels of PWAT for this time of year (1.25" to 1.50") or 
about 5 standard deviations above normal. IVT values also peak at 
around 750 which is a level 3 on the AR scale, though this is 
tempered by the short residence time of the AR. What this all boils 
down to on Sunday is the expectation for widespread shower activity 
with isolated embedded thunderstorms. Given the stronger dynamics 
and lower level 700mb jet around 40 kts, convective activity will be 
capable of bringing down some stronger wind gusts. Precipitation 
amounts Sunday through Sunday night will average 0.50" to 1" for 
Pima, Santa Cruz and Cochise Counties with locales north of Tucson 
including Pinal, Graham and Greenlee Counties along with favored 
southwest flow upslope areas of our Sky Islands more likely to see 
rain amounts ranging from 1 to 2+ inches. A Flash Flood Watch 
remains in effect for 11 PM Saturday through 5 AM Monday for much of 
southeast Arizona. This level of rainfall will result in flowing 
washes, with subsequent increased flows in our river systems into 
early next week as well.

Thereafter, we'll get into a quieter weather regime early next week. 
Any lingering precipitation should come to an end Monday morning with 
shortwave ridging and dry conditions Tuesday and Wednesday. Thursday 
still looks dry as well, then more uncertainty thereafter as another 
system potentially impacts our area next Friday and beyond with more 
precipitation chances. 

Daytimes temperatures will mostly be below normal through the 
forecast period, with the coolest highs Sunday and Monday.
